tagline: Online collaborative whiteboard for diagrams and workshops.
verdictSummary: A personal whiteboard built on an existing open-source canvas SDK — sticky notes, shapes, connectors, autosave — is a real weekend build, not a from-scratch canvas engine. What doesn't come with it is Miro's actual product: reliable performance with dozens of simultaneous editors, a deep template library, and workshop-facilitation tooling.
coreLoopDIY: A personal whiteboard on top of an existing open-source canvas SDK, with named boards, autosave, and PNG/SVG export.
whatYouLose: reliable performance with many simultaneous editors
workshop-facilitation tools like timers and voting
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay for workshops where dozens of people can join a board at once and everything still holds up — not for the ability to draw a sticky note, which open-source canvas tooling already solves.
notes: A good 'kinda': building on an existing canvas SDK makes the demo fast, but production-grade multi-user depth is real, ongoing engineering.
prompt:
Don't write a canvas engine from scratch — build a personal whiteboard on top of an existing open-source canvas SDK (tldraw is a solid choice; it already handles shapes, sticky notes, connectors, and selection well). A board picker for named boards with thumbnails. Autosave each board's canvas state to a database a couple of seconds after the last change, keeping a short history of recent snapshots as undo insurance. Export the current board to PNG and SVG. Seed a handful of starter templates (a retro grid, brainstorm columns, a weekly plan) from simple config files rather than building a template marketplace. Everything works fully offline and locally by default.

Do not build workshop-facilitation tools (timers, voting), third-party integrations, or performance tuning for boards with dozens of simultaneous editors — those are Miro's actual product depth. Real-time sync between exactly two people is a reasonable stretch goal; supporting a whole team on one board at once is not.

faq.q: Can I import my existing Miro boards?
faq.a: Miro exports boards as images or PDFs, which preserve the visual but not the editable shapes. There's no supported way to bring boards back in as live, editable elements.

faq.q: Will it work on my phone?
faq.a: Viewing a board works on a phone browser, but precise shape placement and connector drawing are genuinely harder on a touchscreen — this is realistically a desktop and tablet tool.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Hosting and a database, typically a few dollars a month — no per-seat pricing to think about.

faq.q: What's the one thing that doesn't survive the rebuild?
faq.a: A room full of people editing the same board at once. Real-time multiplayer at Miro's scale needs the same kind of conflict-resolution engineering as Figma's — this build is honestly a personal thinking canvas, not a workshop venue.
